The FCC authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites that work as AI data centers in orbit.
The constellation is called Starmind, and SpaceX must have 10% of it in orbit by 2035.
Only about 17,000 satellites are in space today.

site_article.headline: FCC authorizes SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million data center satellites
site_article.dek: The Starmind approval sets deployment deadlines through 2040 and leaves SpaceX's plans for disposing of high-orbit satellites under review.
site_article.summary: The Federal Communications Commission authorized SpaceX on November 25, 2026, to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million satellites that serve as orbital AI data centers. The license requires 10% of the satellites in orbit by November 2035 and half by November 2038.
site_article.seo_title: FCC approves SpaceX Starmind: 1 million AI satellites
site_article.seo_description: The FCC authorized SpaceX to launch up to 1 million Starmind satellites as AI data centers in orbit. The deadlines, the hardware and who opposed the plan.
site_article.answer_summary: Yes. On November 25, 2026, the FCC authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites that act as data centers in orbit, with deployment milestones running to 2040.

paragraphs.text: The Federal Communications Commission said on November 25, 2026, that it had authorized SpaceX to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million satellites designed to work as data centers in orbit, according to Reuters. The constellation is called Starmind, and the FCC said the approval is meant to help meet fast growing demand for AI computing.

SpaceX filed the original application on January 30, 2026, according to Latin Times, and described the project as a step toward a Kardashev Type II civilization, one that captures the energy of its star. Latin Times called the order the first regulatory approval of its kind in the United States.

The license sets firm milestones. SpaceX must have a first satellite operating by November 25, 2033, deploy 10% of the maximum, or 100,000 satellites, by November 2035, and reach half of the constellation by November 2038, Reuters reported. Latin Times and Lynnwood Times reported that the full constellation is due by 2040, and that the authorization becomes void if the deadlines are missed.

The scale is far beyond anything in orbit now. Reuters noted that only about 17,000 satellites are in space, and that SpaceX's Starlink network has just over 11,000. SpaceX once sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it started that system, and operators often ask for more satellites than they end up launching.

According to Lynnwood Times, the first generation unit, called AI1, has a deployed height of about 30 meters, a solar array wingspan of up to 75 meters and a mass of up to 4,000 kilograms. Each carries Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 class computing hardware rated up to 250 kilowatts at peak and about 175 kilowatts on average, cooled by liquid radiators and grouped in clusters of about 10 units.

The satellites will fly in shells between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, in sun-synchronous and 30-degree orbits, and talk to each other and to Starlink over optical links. The FCC also approved radio frequencies as a backup to that optical network. SpaceX plans to build the satellites at a facility in Bastrop, Texas, and launch them on Starship, and Elon Musk has said the first Starmind computers could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of 2027.

Amazon's satellite unit, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society formally opposed the application, Latin Times reported. Amazon and others argued that SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all of the satellites. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr rejected that criticism in March, Reuters reported, and the commission dismissed the astronomers' concerns as outside the scope of the proceeding, according to Latin Times.

One question remains open. The FCC deferred SpaceX's request to dispose of satellites above 600 kilometers in other orbits instead of letting them burn up in the atmosphere, and SpaceX must file more debris mitigation details before it operates satellites at those altitudes. Carr celebrated the decision on X, and Musk replied that Starmind will be a great asset to America and the world.

The license gives SpaceX room to try something no company has done at scale, but the milestones are the real test. Even the 2035 target of 100,000 satellites is several times the number of satellites in orbit today, and it depends on Starship delivering cheap, frequent launches.
The first checkpoint is whether Starmind hardware reaches orbit in 2027, as Musk has suggested, and whether the FCC accepts SpaceX's plan for disposing of satellites above 600 kilometers.
